overview.title: Nanopore-Based Molecular Sensing
overview.focus: My research explores nanopore-based molecular sensing strategies for the quantitative and multiplexed detection of low-abundance disease-associated biomarkers. I am particularly interested in developing molecular recognition, signal-generation, and quantitative measurement approaches that could contribute to earlier and more reliable disease detection.

entries.title: Reference-Based DNA Barcode Quantification
entries.institution: Imperial College London · Current MSci research
entries.description: Investigating reference-based DNA quantification using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT). By comparing sequence-distinguishable DNA barcodes with an internal reference, this work explores strategies to improve the accuracy, precision, and reliability of nanopore-based concentration measurements.
entries.status: Current experimental research: accuracy, precision and quantitative reproducibility. Research question: when does an internal reference improve concentration estimates, and how do barcode-dependent responses affect the result?
entries.alt: B1 target and B3 internal reference enter a biological nanopore sequencing workflow, followed by sequence identification and relative quantification.
entries.caption: B1 target and B3 reference are distinguished by sequence. Their relative read counts inform concentration estimates through calibration.

entries.title: Enzyme-Mediated RNA Detection and Signal Amplification
entries.institution: Imperial College London · Parallel MSci research direction
entries.description: Exploring enzyme-assisted detection of low-abundance RNA biomarkers through DNA–RNA hybridisation and Duplex DNase-mediated cleavage. This strategy investigates sequence-encoded DNA reporter generation, potential RNA recycling and signal amplification, and opportunities for multiplexed molecular detection.
entries.status: Proposed strategy: target-dependent reporter production and amplification remain to be validated. This independent direction also explores quantitative RNA detection through appropriate assay-specific calibration.

pages.title: Reference-Based DNA Barcode Quantification
pages.intro: Improving the accuracy, precision and reliability of DNA concentration measurements through sequence-distinguishable target and reference barcodes.

sections.title: Scientific background
sections.lead: Measuring molecular abundance through sequence-based readout.
sections.body:
ONT sequencing provides molecular identity and read counts. My current synthetic DNA work asks how distinguishable target and reference barcodes can support concentration measurements that are accurate, precise and reproducible. Quantitative performance depends on how molecules reach the pore, generate usable reads and receive a sequence assignment.

This direction is independent of enzyme-mediated RNA detection. Both investigate quantitative molecular sensing, and each requires calibration appropriate to its own workflow.

sections.title: ONT sequencing principles
sections.lead: ONT sequencing couples controlled nucleic-acid movement to electrical measurement.
sections.body:
An engineered protein pore sits within a membrane under an applied potential. A motor protein regulates DNA movement so that the electrical signal can be recorded as the strand passes through the sensing region.

Current depends on the local nucleotide context occupying the pore. Basecalling models interpret that signal as a nucleotide sequence. Matching the read to a known sequence library then allows DNA barcodes to identify distinguishable molecular reporters. [1]
figures: ont-readout
Motor-regulated DNA transport, sequence-dependent current and basecalling
Figure 03 Molecular transport, signal generation and sequence assignment are distinct steps. Current levels reflect local sequence context rather than independent one-base signals.
sections.after:
Sequence as an identifier

A barcode is a chosen DNA sequence. A recognition probe can associate a particular target with that sequence, allowing chemically different targets to share a nucleic-acid readout. [4]

Identity is not abundance

A correct sequence assignment tells us which reporter was read. Inferring the original target amount also requires suitable controls, calibration and an understanding of the conversion and detection steps.

sections.title: DNA barcode design
sections.lead: B1 is the target barcode. B3 is an internal reference at a known concentration.
sections.body: The supplied B1/B3 designs share a common region and contain different barcode-specific sequences. Classification against those distinguishable sequences assigns reads to B1 or B3, enabling separate counting. A complementary C-strand pairs antiparallel to the common region.
figures: barcode-reference
B1 target and B3 reference architectures with common and barcode-specific regions

Figure 04 Both designs contain a 15-nt common region and a 35-nt barcode-specific region. Complementary C-strands pair antiparallel to the common region, with a 3′ A overhang. Region lengths describe molecular architecture, not assay performance. The schematic does not specify library preparation.

sections.title: Reference-based measurement
sections.lead: How can internal reference barcodes improve the accuracy, precision and reliability of DNA concentration estimates?
sections.body: B1 and B3 can already be identified and counted through sequence-based readout. The research question concerns the reliability of the concentration estimate obtained from those counts. An internal reference of known concentration supports a relative measurement, subject to calibration.
sections.after:
REFERENCE NORMALISATION

R = NB1 / NB3

CB1 = (R / α) × CB3

N denotes classified read counts, C denotes concentration, and α is the relative detection response factor established through calibration. The expression assumes a calibrated proportional response over the range in which it is applied.

What a reference can help with

Comparing counts within the same sequencing workflow may reduce the effect of shared changes in overall sequencing output. The ratio connects relative barcode abundance to a known reference.

What calibration must address

Capture, sequence context, preparation, recovery and classification can affect B1 and B3 differently. Reference normalisation does not automatically remove those effects. Reliable estimation requires controls, repeat measurements and independent validation.

sections.title: Quantitative measurement challenges
sections.lead: A reference can reduce some shared variation while leaving differential responses and uncertainty.
sections.body:
Sequencing output and response

Sequencing duration, active pores and sample preparation affect total output. B1 and B3 may also differ in capture, recovery, sequence context or usable-read generation. A ratio does not automatically cancel barcode-specific effects.

Sequence classification

Read quality, sequence coverage and classification criteria determine which reads enter each count. More accepted reads need not mean a more accurate concentration estimate if incorrect assignments also increase.

Counting uncertainty

Finite counts introduce sampling uncertainty in both numerator and denominator. Sparse target counts limit precision, while sparse reference counts can destabilise the ratio. This uncertainty is distinct from systematic bias.

Calibration and reproducibility

Known standards, blanks, single-barcode controls and independent repeats help assess response factors, background and consistency. Accuracy concerns closeness to the known value; precision concerns repeated-measurement spread. Reproducibility tests whether results remain consistent across independent measurements.

sections.title: Research questions
sections.lead: The emphasis is on measurement reliability rather than a claim that abundance counting is new.
sections.body:
• When does internal reference normalisation improve accuracy or precision, and when does it introduce additional variability?
  • How do barcode sequence design, capture and classification affect relative detection response?
  • What controls and calibration support reproducible concentration estimates for low-abundance DNA?

sections.title: Nanopore sensing context
sections.lead: Two pore architectures share an electrical sensing principle.
sections.body:
An applied potential drives ions through the pore. When a molecule enters, passes through or interacts with the opening, it changes ionic transport. The resulting current modulation provides a way to observe individual molecular events.

Biological pores use a protein channel in a membrane. Solid-state pores use an opening in an artificial solid membrane. Their shared electrical foundation supports different approaches to identification, quantitative sensing and biomedical research. [1] [2]
figures: pore-comparison
Biological and solid-state nanopores, with molecular transport and conceptual current traces
Figure 01 Two pore architectures, one electrical principle. Cross-sections are conceptual and not to scale. Every trace on this page is illustrative, not an experimental recording.

pages.provenance: The B1/B3 design and quantitative research questions follow Yihan Li’s supplied MSci project presentation. Enzyme-mediated RNA detection is a separate, parallel research direction.

pages.title: Enzyme-Mediated RNA Detection
pages.intro: Exploring RNA recognition, Duplex DNase-mediated DNA cleavage, proposed reporter generation and potential signal amplification.

sections.title: Scientific motivation
sections.lead: Low-abundance RNA biomarkers present a problem of recognition, background and quantitative reliability.
sections.body:
Circulating miRNAs can provide information about biological and disease-associated processes. Low abundance, degradation and a complex molecular background complicate detection and interpretation. The proposed strategy explores chemical recognition and reporter generation as a route to a sequence-based readout.

Liquid biopsy examines molecular biomarkers in accessible biofluids, offering minimally invasive sampling and the possibility of repeated measurements. Circulating DNA, RNA and proteins can provide complementary information about biological processes. [3]

Low abundance, degradation and complex sample backgrounds can make a disease-associated signal difficult to distinguish from other molecules. A sensitive sensor must also establish what it detected and whether its readout supports a reliable concentration estimate.
figures: biomarker-workflow
Four stages from disease-associated molecular changes to nanopore readout
Figure 02 Molecular recognition connects the biomarker to an interpretable readout. This is a conceptual analytical workflow, not a clinical diagnostic pathway.
sections.after: Early molecular detection is a research motivation. Analytical sensitivity alone does not establish screening benefit, disease specificity or clinical utility.

sections.title: Molecular recognition
sections.lead: A complementary DNA region binds the model RNA target miR-21-5p.
sections.body:
Complementary base pairing brings DNA and RNA together as an antiparallel hybrid. The recognition sequence determines which RNA is addressed; the barcode sequence encodes the identity of the reporter. The model RNA in the supplied design is miR-21-5p, matched to the linked miRBase record. [6]

RNA-probe architecture and proposed cleavage concepts are informed by Minghui Qi’s viva and the MSci project presentation. They are not presented as individually demonstrated experimental achievements.

sections.title: DNA probe architecture
sections.lead: Recognition and signal encoding occupy different functional regions.
sections.body: The supplied probe includes a UNI code and ID code for signal encoding, an LSP region, a complementary RNA-recognition region and an anchor. These design labels do not by themselves establish protective or structural functions: LSP protection and the anchor’s experimental role require protocol confirmation.
figures: rna-probe
Five functional regions of the 83-nt probe and the miR-21-5p target sequence

Figure 05 Source-supported probe architecture: UNI code, ID code, LSP, complementary recognition region and anchor. The 24-nt RNA sequence matches the supplied design and miRBase MIMAT0000076. [6] LSP protection and the anchor’s experimental role require confirmation.

sections.title: Duplex DNase-mediated cleavage
sections.lead: General substrate behaviour does not establish the outcome of a particular probe design.
sections.body:
Duplex DNase preferentially degrades duplex DNA and can cleave the DNA strand of a DNA–RNA hybrid. The enzyme acts on an appropriate duplex substrate; complementary probe binding supplies the sequence selectivity. [5]

For this proposed assay, the location and extent of DNA cleavage, release of the RNA and survival of the barcode-containing region remain experimental questions. No exact cleavage sites or verified reporter ends are assigned.

sections.title: Proposed DNA reporter generation
sections.lead: Target-dependent cleavage could produce a DNA fragment containing an identifiable barcode.
sections.body: The intended output is a barcode-containing DNA reporter. Its sequence identity, terminal structure, length distribution, integrity and recovery must be verified. A molecular design alone does not establish that an intact, sequence-compatible reporter is produced.
figures: rna-reaction
Six-step proposed mechanism with explicit DNA–RNA antiparallel pairing and unverified RNA recycling

Figure 06 Proposed recognition, cleavage and readout pathway. DNA runs 5′→3′ across the page and its paired RNA runs 3′→5′. Dashed DNA segments denote unspecified cleavage products, not assigned cut sites. The reporter endpoint and RNA recycling remain unverified.

sections.title: Potential RNA recycling and signal amplification
sections.lead: The same RNA may participate in further probe-recognition and cleavage cycles.
sections.body:
If RNA survives cleavage and dissociates from DNA fragments, it could bind a fresh probe. Repeated participation could generate more than one reporter per target RNA. This is proposed target recycling, not RNA replication or an exponential amplification scheme.

Repeated turnover, the number of intact reporters, background generation and response to reaction time need validation before making an amplification or sensitivity claim.
sections.nav: Potential RNA recycling and signal amplification

sections.title: Multiplexed molecular detection
sections.lead: Distinct recognition regions could be associated with different reporter barcodes.
sections.body:
In principle, one probe could recognise RNA A and encode barcode A, while another recognises RNA B and encodes barcode B. Sequence assignment could then separate their reporter populations within a shared readout. Cross-recognition, background cleavage, reporter recovery and classification would need assessment across the probe set.

Multiplexing is a research objective for the proposed RNA assay. It is not a demonstrated result of this project. Related published barcoded-probe work provides broader context. [4]

sections.title: ONT readout and quantitative calibration
sections.lead: The RNA strategy can support quantitative investigation through its own suitable calibration.
sections.body:
After stopping the reaction and verifying products, an appropriate library must make the reporter compatible with ONT sequencing. Short DNA fragments are not automatically suitable for motor-controlled sequencing. Adapter compatibility, any C-strand use and reference-addition timing require protocol confirmation.

Basecalling and sequence classification could identify and count reporter populations. Known RNA standards must pass through the complete reaction, recovery, library and sequencing workflow to relate that readout to original RNA input. Reporter concentration and read counts are different quantities from target RNA concentration.

Enzyme-mediated RNA detection is independent of the B1/B3 DNA quantification direction. B1/B3 experiments are not a prerequisite. The RNA assay requires calibration of its own complete response.

sections.title: Research questions
sections.lead: Recognition, signal generation and measurement each need their own evidence.
sections.body:
• Does target recognition lead to specific, recoverable barcode-containing reporters?
  • Can the same RNA undergo repeated productive cycles, and what background accompanies reporter generation?
  • Can distinguishable probe barcodes support selective multiplexing?
  • How does the complete calibrated readout relate to RNA input, with suitable precision and reproducibility?

sections.title: Broader group context
sections.lead: Related strategies use different ways to connect recognition to an electrical or sequence signal.
sections.body:
The supplied viva also explores binding-induced strand displacement, in which target binding changes probe pairing to release or expose a DNA barcode, and delay sensing, in which a target bound to a probe changes translocation dynamics. These are distinct from the proposed Duplex DNase conversion pathway.

Combining recognition elements for RNA, DNA and proteins could connect different biomarker classes to a common readout. These are broader research directions presented by Minghui Qi and the research group. They are not claims about my individual experimental contributions. Published barcoded-probe work provides related scientific context. [4]

pages.provenance: The current project presentation is the primary scientific source. Minghui Qi’s supplied viva provides broader group context and the probe architecture. Proposed reporter generation, RNA recycling and multiplexing have not been presented here as validated outcomes.

pages.title: Solid-State Nanopore Sensing
pages.intro: Established sensing principles, with space for confirmed details of my research experience.

sections.title: Solid-state nanopore principles
sections.lead: Artificial apertures connect electrolyte solutions across a solid membrane.
sections.body:
With electrolyte on both sides and a potential across the membrane, ions pass through the opening. A molecule interacting with the pore can change the current. Event depth and duration provide features for investigating transport and molecular interactions.

Geometry, surface properties, solution conditions and molecular size, charge and conformation influence the response. Tunable pore architecture offers experimental flexibility, while fast transport, noise, adsorption and pore-to-pore variation can complicate interpretation. [2]
figures: solid-state
Artificial membrane, electrolyte, applied voltage, molecular translocation and illustrative current blockade

Figure 07 A generic solid-state sensing configuration. The blockade shape is illustrative. Molecular events may produce different current responses depending on the pore and solution conditions; no Zhejiang-specific material or device is implied.

sections.title: Molecular translocation and current signatures
sections.lead: A current event reflects interactions between a molecule, the pore and its environment.
sections.body:
An applied potential drives ionic current through the pore. Molecular entry, passage or interaction can change that current. The event depth and duration provide information about transport, but their interpretation depends on molecular properties, pore geometry, surface interactions and solution conditions.

The blockade shown here is an illustrative signal rather than a measurement. Other current responses can occur under different conditions. A generic blockade does not provide the sequence-resolution capability of ONT basecalling.

sections.title: Applications and limitations
sections.lead: Solid-state nanopores support investigations of molecular transport and sensing.
sections.body:
Artificial pore geometries and surfaces offer flexibility for studying nucleic acids, proteins and other molecular systems. Identification may require additional recognition chemistry or carefully characterised electrical features.

Fast transport, electrical noise, nonspecific adsorption and pore-to-pore variation can limit interpretation. A sensing event alone does not establish target identity, concentration or clinical utility. [2]

sections.title: Biological and solid-state nanopores compared
sections.lead: Both approaches measure ionic transport at the nanoscale. What that signal can tell us depends on the pore and the assay.
sections.body:
PROTEIN CHANNEL

Biological nanopores / ONT

Structure
Engineered protein pore in a membrane.
Transport & signal
A motor regulates nucleic-acid movement. Sequence context modulates current.
Identification
Basecalling and sequence matching support barcode identity. Recognition probes can connect other analytes to that identity.
Flexibility & limits
Protein engineering and probe design offer selectivity. Suitable molecular constructs, library compatibility and calibration constrain the assay.

ARTIFICIAL APERTURE

Solid-state nanopores

Structure
Nanoscale opening in an artificial solid membrane.
Transport & signal
Transport and interactions produce event features such as current change and duration.
Identification
Interpretation depends on signal features and any additional recognition chemistry. A blockade alone does not provide ONT-like sequence resolution.
Flexibility & limits
Pore geometry and surface chemistry can be adjusted. Transport control, noise and nonspecific interactions remain important challenges.

This comparison concerns ONT-style sequencing and generic solid-state ionic-current sensing. It does not imply that all biological pores sequence DNA, or that all nanopore platforms have equivalent capabilities. [1] [2]
